entities.name: Wars of the Roses
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Wars of the Roses was a dynastic civil war in the Kingdom of England, fought between the houses of Lancaster and York from 1455 to 1487. This pivotal conflict marked a turning point in English history, as the rival claimants to the throne, Richard Plantagenet, 3rd Duke of York, and Henry VI, ultimately led to the downfall of the Lancastrian dynasty and the rise of the Tudors. The war was marked by some of the most infamous battles in English history, including the Battle of Towton, which remains the bloodiest single-day battle ever fought in England. The Wars of the Roses shaped the course of English history, leading to the eventual accession of the Tudor dynasty and the rise of the English monarchy as we know it today.

The conflict began in 1455, when Richard, Duke of York, claimed the throne, citing his descent from Lionel of Antwerp, the second son of King Edward III. The Lancastrian king, Henry VI, was seen as weak and ineffective, and the Duke of York's claim was backed by many nobles who were dissatisfied with the king's rule. The conflict escalated over the next several years, with both sides suffering significant losses. The war was marked by brutal fighting, siege warfare, and the use of mercenaries. The eventual victor, Henry Tudor, would go on to become King Henry VII, marking the beginning of the Tudor dynasty.

The Wars of the Roses had significant consequences for the English monarchy and the course of English history. The conflict led to the rise of the Tudors, who would go on to produce some of the most famous monarchs in English history, including Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. The war also led to the decline of the nobility and the rise of the common people, who would eventually come to dominate English politics. The Wars of the Roses remain one of the most fascinating and complex periods in English history, marked by intrigue, betrayal, and ultimately, the rise of a new dynasty.
